parts.problemMd:
A student used a force meter attached to one end of a uniform metre rule to determine the mass of a block. The centre of the metre rule is attached to a stand about which it can pivot.

A block of unknown mass $m$ can be attached to the metre rule through one of the small holes, as shown.

![A metre rule balanced on a central pivot stand, with a force meter attached at the zero mark on the left end and small holes at the 60, 70, 80 and 90 cm marks. A block of unknown mass m is at rest on the ground.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/moments/assets/003-a-metre-rule-balanced-on-a-central-pivot-stand-w.png)

The student attached the block to each small hole and adjusted the force meter to make it vertical before taking a reading.

Explain how the student could check the metre rule is horizontal before taking a reading.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **pair** from (1 mark per point):
> 
> - Use two set squares, one in contact with the bench and the other with the metre rule
> - Check at both ends / at two different points
> 
> **OR**
> 
> - Measure the height of the metre rule above the bench using a second rule and a set square
> - Check at both ends / at two different points
> 
> **OR**
> 
> - Use a spirit level
> - Check bubble is in the middle / check in more than one position
> 
> **[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The student places the block at the $80\text{cm}$ mark and pulls the force meter vertically downwards until the ruler is horizontal. The reading on the force meter is $1.45\text{N}$.

Calculate the mass $m$ of the block. You should take moments about the pivot.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass $m$ of the block:

- List the known quantities:

  - Force reading, $F=1.45\text{N}$
  - Weight of block, $W=mg$
  - Distance of force meter from pivot$=50\text{cm}$
  - Distance of mass from pivot $=80-50=30\text{cm}$
  - $g=9.81\text{N kg}^{-1}$
- The moment due to force $F$ about the pivot is:

moment $=Fx$

anticlockwise moment $=F\times50$ **[1 mark]**

- The moment due to weight $W$ about the pivot is:

clockwise moment $= W \times \left(80 - 50\right)$

clockwise moment $=mg\times30$ **[1 mark]**

- Apply the principle of moments about the pivot:

clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments

$mg\times30=1.45\times50$ **[1 mark]**

$m=\frac{1.45\times50}{9.81\times30}$

$m=$ $0.25\text{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for use of moment = $Fx$
> 
> 1 mark for use of $F=mg$
> 
> 1 mark for applying the principle of moments about the pivot
> 
> 1 mark for a final answer of $m=0.25\text{kg}$

parts.problemMd:
The student wants to reduce the percentage uncertainty in the value obtained for the mass of the block.

The student moved the force meter towards the centre of gravity of the metre rule and repeated the measurements.

Deduce whether the percentage uncertainty in the value obtained for the mass of the block is reduced by the student moving the force meter. No calculations are required.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - The distance to the pivot would decrease 
> **OR** 
> The percentage uncertainty in distance would increase **[1 mark]**
> 
> - The force meter reading would increase 
> **OR** 
> The percentage uncertainty in force would decrease **[1 mark]**
> 
> - (Since one increases and the other decreases) we cannot be sure how the percentage uncertainty would change **[1 mark]**
> 
> The third mark is dependent on scoring the first two marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This type of question tests your ability to reason qualitatively about uncertainties without performing calculations. Make sure you consider the effect on each variable separately before drawing an overall conclusion.

parts.problemMd:
A dragster is a racing car designed for a very short race along a completely straight track, so must be able to accelerate at a very high rate. The dragster and driver shown below have a combined weight of 1.23 × 10<sup>4</sup> N. The centre of gravity is 1.80 m in front of the rear axle.

![q16-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/moments/assets/009-q16-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-ph.png)

The front axle of the dragster is 6.00 m from the rear axle.

Calculate the reaction forces *R*<sub>1</sub> and *R*<sub>2</sub>, shown on the diagram, when the dragster is stationary and not accelerating.

*R*<sub>1</sub> = ................................

*R*<sub>2</sub> = ................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the reaction forces *R*<sub>1</sub> and *R*<sub>2</sub>:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from the weight to *R*<sub>1</sub> = 4.20 m
- Distance from the weight to *R*<sub>2</sub> = 1.80 m
- Distance from from to rear axle = 6.00 m
- Weight = 1.23 × 10<sup>4</sup> N

Calculate *R*<sub>1</sub> by taking moments about the rear axle:

- $moment=Fx$
- Clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments (since the car is in equilibrium) **[1 mark]**
- $\left(1 . 23 \times 10^{4}\right) \times 1 . 80 = R_{1} \times 6 . 00$ **[1 mark]**
- *R*<sub>1</sub> = 3.69 × 10<sup>3</sup> N

Calculate *R*<sub>2</sub> by taking moments about the front axle:

- $R_{2} \times 6 . 00 = \left(1 . 23 \times 10^{4}\right) \times 4 . 20$
- *R*<sub>2</sub> = 8.61 × 10<sup>3</sup> N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You can take moments about any pivot, you will be expected to choose your own*

  - *The reason **R*<sub>*1*</sub>* is calculated by taking moments about the rear axle is that we don't know **R*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Therefore, using the rear axle (where **R*<sub>*2*</sub>*) as the pivot means that **R*<sub>*2 *</sub>*doesn't turn up in the moment conservation equation*

parts.problemMd:
When the dragster starts, there is a driving force that gives the dragster an initial forward acceleration of 5.50 g.

Calculate the initial driving force on the dragster.

Initial driving force = ...............................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the initial driving force on the dragster:

List the known quantities:

- Acceleration = 5.50 *g*
- Weight = 1.23 × 10<sup>4</sup> N

Calculate the force on the dragster:

- $m=\frac{W}{g}=\frac{1.23\times10^{4}}{g}$
- $ΣF=ma=\frac{1.23\times10^{4}}{g}\times5.50\timesg$** [1 mark]**
- Initial driving force = 6.77 × 10<sup>4</sup> N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The power from the car’s engine is constant.

Explain how the force from the engine varies as the car accelerates.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain how the force from the engine varies as the car accelerates:

- Since $P=\frac{W}{t}$ **OR** $\DeltaW=F\Deltas$ **[1 mark]**
- Since $\frac{\Deltas}{t}=v$, combining these gives $P=\frac{F\Deltas}{t}=Fv$
- The force will decrease as the velocity increases; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *If you are asked to compare how one variable changes with another, try and determine the equation that **links them both*
- *In this case, it is the power **P** and the force **F*

  - *P** = **Fv** is a common equation you can memorise*
  - *It is only used when there is a **constant velocity*

parts.problemMd:
A large parasol has been set up on a windy day. The centre of gravity of the parasol is vertically above the centre of the base. The bottom of the parasol starts to lift from the ground as shown. The weight of the parasol is 110 N.

![q19-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/moments/assets/004-q19-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level.png)

The force of the wind is 14 N in a horizontal direction.

![q19a-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/moments/assets/005-q19a-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-leve.png)

Explain why the parasol will topple. Your answer should include a calculation.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain why the parasol will topple. Your answer should include a calculation:

List the known quantities:

- Weight of parasol, $W$ = 110 N
- Force of wind, $F$ = 14 N
- Height of parasol, $h$ = 1.80 m
- Width of base, $w$ = 0.44 m

Use the moment equation:

- $\mathrm{moment}=Fx$
- $A n t i - c l o c k w i s e \left(A C W\right) moment from wind = F h = 14 \times 1 . 80$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the clockwise (CW) and anticlockwise (ACW) moments:

- $\mathrm{ACW} \mathrm{moment} \mathrm{from} \mathrm{wind}=25.2Nm$ **AND**
- $\mathrm{CW} \mathrm{moment} \mathrm{from} \mathrm{base}=110\times0.22=24.2Nm$ **[1 mark]**

Describe the moments as the angle of the parasol changes:

- As angle to the ground increases, clockwise moment from the weight decreases; **OR**
- If line of action of weight moves outside base cannot regain equilibrium; **[1 mark]**

Compare the moments:

- 25.2 N m > 24.2 N m <u>therefore</u> the parasol blows over; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *We are told that the base has **already** started lifting - your explanation must include what happens **as the base lifts** (this is the third mark)*
- *It is important to identify the **pivot** in any moments question - in this case it is the **left side** of the base that the parasol rotates about*

  - *As the parasol rotates, the **maximum** perpendicular distance from the pivot to the weight force is 0.22 m (half the base)*
  - *This **reduces** as the parasol rotates*

![screenshot-2023-01-16-at-12-29-07](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/moments/assets/006-screenshot-2023-01-16-at-12-29-07.png)

![screenshot-2023-01-16-at-12-33-28](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/moments/assets/007-screenshot-2023-01-16-at-12-33-28.png)

parts.problemMd:
To prevent the parasol from toppling, a rope is attached to the parasol at 1.50 m from the ground as shown. The rope makes an angle of 44° to the vertical.

![q19b-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/moments/assets/008-q19b-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-leve.png)

The horizontal force from the wind is now 25 N.

Determine, by taking moments about the centre of the base, the vertical force that the base exerts on the ground.

Assume that the force which the ground exerts on the base acts through the midpoint of the base.

Force exerted on the ground = ..........................................
parts.solutionMd:
Determine, by taking moments about the centre of the base, the vertical force that the base exerts on the ground:

List the known quantities:

- Force of wind, $F$ = 25 N
- Height of parasol, $h$ = 1.80 m
- Weight of parasol, $W$ = 110 N
- Vertical height of rope, $l_{vert}$ = 1.50 m
- Angle of rope to parasol = 44°

Write the horizontal component of tension, $T_{hor}$, in terms of $T$:

- $T_{h o r} = T sin \left(44 \circ\right)$ **[1 mark]**

Equate moments about the centre of the base to determine $T$:

- $CW moment = T_{h o r} l_{v e r t} = 1 . 50 T sin \left(44 \circ\right)$
- $\mathrm{ACW} \mathrm{moment}=Fh=45Nm$
- $45 = 1 . 50 T sin \left(44 \circ\right)$ **[1 mark]**
- $T = \frac{45}{1 . 50 sin \left(44 \circ\right)} = 43 . 2 N$

Determine the vertical component of tension, $T_{vert}$:

- $T_{v e r t} = T cos \left(44 \circ\right) = 43 . 2 cos \left(44 \circ\right) = 31 . 1 N$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the total force on the ground:

- $\mathrm{total} \mathrm{force}=W+T_{vert}=110+31.1$ **[1 mark]**
- $\mathrm{total} \mathrm{force} \mathrm{on} \mathrm{ground}=141.1=140N$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *If you are unsure where to start - work **backwards*

  - *We are trying to find the total downwards force through the base*
  - *We must find the downwards force due to **tension** and add it to weight*
  - $T$* can only be calculated by equating the wind moment and the tension moment*
  - *Use this to find the **vertical component **of tension and add this to weight*
- *The assumption "force which the ground exerts on the base acts through the midpoint of the base" allows us to ignore any moments from a **reaction** **force** at the **edges** of the base - we can imagine **only a small point** of the parasol touches the ground*

parts.problemMd:
A sledge accelerates, due to gravity, from rest down a frictionless slope. Air resistance can be ignored. The slope is at an angle of 6.9° to the horizontal, as shown.

![screenshot-2023-01-12-at-14-58-13](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/022-screenshot-2023-01-12-at-14-58-13.png)

Complete the free‐body force diagram below for the sledge.

`⚫`
parts.solutionMd:
Complete the free‐body force diagram below for the sledge:

![screenshot-2023-01-12-at-15-04-06](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/023-screenshot-2023-01-12-at-15-04-06.png)

- Vertical downwards force labelled "weight" / "W";
- Force perpendicular to slope (by eye) labelled "reaction" / "R" **OR** "(normal) contact" / "N";

- *The reaction force **must** be clearly perpendicular to the slope*

  - *This means it is 6.9° to the right of vertical*
- *The range of accepted reaction force directions is shown below*

![screenshot-2023-01-12-at-15-21-37](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/024-screenshot-2023-01-12-at-15-21-37.png)

parts.problemMd:
The slope has a total length of 60m

i) Show that the initial acceleration of the sledge along the slope is about 1 m s<sup>−2</sup>

Initial acceleration = ........................................ **(2)**

ii) Determine the speed of the sledge at the end of the slope.

Speed at end of slope = .................................... **(2)**

iii) Determine the time taken for the sledge to travel to the end of the slope.

**    **                           Time taken = ...................................... **(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) Show that the initial acceleration of the sledge along the slope is about 1 m s<sup>–2</sup>:

List the known quantities:

- Acceleration of free fall, $g$ = 9.81 m s<sup>-2</sup>
- Angle of the slope to horizontal = 6.9°

Find the component of $g$ along the slope:

- $a = g sin \left(6 . 9 \circ\right)$ **[1 mark]**
- $a=1.18ms^{-2}=1.2ms^{-2}$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

ii) Determine the speed of the sledge at the end of the slope:

List the known and unknown suvat quantities:

- $s$ = 60 m
- $u$ = 0 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- $v$ = to be calculated
- $a$ = 1.18 m s<sup>-2</sup> (from part **(b)(i)**)
- $t$ = ?

Choose a suvat equation and rearrange for $v$:

- $v^{2}=u^{2}+2as$
- $u=0ms^{-1}$ so $v=\sqrt{2as}$
- $v=\sqrt{2\times1.18\times60}=11.90ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\mathrm{final} \mathrm{speed}=12ms^{-1}$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

iii) Determine the time taken for the sledge to travel to the end of the slope:

List the known and unknown suvat quantities:

- $s$ = 60 m
- $u$ = 0 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- $v$ = 11.9 m s<sup>-1</sup> (from part **(b)(ii)**)
- $a$ = 1.18 m s<sup>-2</sup> (from part **(b)(i)**)
- $t$ = to be calculated

Choose a suvat equation and rearrange for $t$:

- $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
- $u=0ms^{-1}$ so $s=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
- $t=\sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times60}{1.18}}=10.1s$ **[1 mark]**
- Time taken = 10 s (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *In part (i), drawing a diagram can help you understand how to calculate the component of acceleration along the slope*

![screenshot-2023-01-12-at-16-07-51](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/025-screenshot-2023-01-12-at-16-07-51.png)

- *Some quick trigonometry then reveals why the component down the slope is *$g sin \left(6 . 9 \circ\right)$

![screenshot-2023-01-12-at-16-13-05](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/026-screenshot-2023-01-12-at-16-13-05.png)

- *Part (ii) can also be solved by equating increase in the kinetic energy store with decrease in the GPE store (ensuring that the vertical height is used, not 60 m) - have a go and see if you end up with the same result*
- *Part (iii) can be solved using *$v=u+at$*, as **t** is the only unknown suvat quantity here*

parts.problemMd:
A trolley accelerates from rest at point A, down a straight track to point B. The trolley then continues along a horizontal track to point C, as shown.

![q12-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/027-q12-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-ph.png)

The effects of air resistance and friction are negligible.

Show that the trolley reaches point B with a speed of about 3 m s<sup>−1</sup> .
parts.solutionMd:
To show that the trolley reaches point B with a speed of about 3 m s<sup>−1</sup>:

List the known quantities:

- Initial height = 0.50 m

From the data booklet:

- Acceleration of free fall *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>

Equate gravitational potential at the end with final kinetic energy:

- $mgh=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\cancel{m} g h = \frac{1}{2} \cancel{m} v^{2}$

Substitute in known values and calculate final velocity:

- $gh=\frac{1}{2}v^{2}$
- $9.81\times0.5=\frac{1}{2}v^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v = \sqrt{\left(2 \times 9 . 81 \times 0 . 5\right)}$
- $v=3.13ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *There is an alternative method to this problem using SUVAT*
- *First you would need to find the **parallel** component of **g** and the **distance** along the ramp*

  - *Then substitute into *$v^{2}=u^{2}+2as$
- *Whilst this is a perfectly valid method it involves more steps and therefore we recommend using gravitational and kinetic energy equivalence as shown in the mark scheme above*

parts.problemMd:
Determine the time taken by the object to move from point A to point C.

Time taken = ..........................
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the time taken by the object to move from point A to point C:

List the known quantities:

- Height of ramp, *h* = 0.5 m
- Horizontal length of ramp, *s* = 2.0 m
- Initial speed of the object, *u* = 0
- Final speed of the object, *v *= 3.13 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Determine the distance travelled using Pythagoras:

- $a=\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}}=\sqrt{s^{2}+h^{2}}=\sqrt{2.0^{2}+0.5^{2}}=2.06m$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the time taken to travel down the ramp from point A to B:

- $s = \frac{1}{2} \left(u + v\right) t$
- $2 . 06 = \frac{1}{2} \left(0 + 3 . 13\right) t_{A B}$
- $t_{AB}=1.32s$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the time taken to travel from point B to C:

- $s=vt$
- $t_{BC}=\frac{s}{v}=\frac{1.0}{3.13}=0.32s$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total time:

- $t_{total}=t_{AB}+t_{BC}=1.32+0.32$
- Time taken = 1.64 s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The key to this question is working through each stage separately before combining them*
- *A common mistake is trying to do the whole calculation in one step which will lead to errors due to the difference in average speed across each section AB and BC.*

parts.problemMd:
A skier moving at 25 m s<sup>−1</sup> skis off a ramp. The ramp is angled upwards at 10° to the horizontal, as shown.

There is a flat surface that starts 30 m from the ramp. The flat surface is 2.9 m below the ramp.

![q14-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/021-q14-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-ph.png)

Deduce whether the skier reaches the flat surface before landing. You may ignore any effects of air resistance.
parts.solutionMd:
To deduce whether the skier reaches the flat surface before landing:

List the known quantities:

- Height of ramp = 2.9 m
- Horizontal distance to the bottom of the ramp = 30 m
- Initial speed = 25 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Angle of take-off = 10 °

From the data booklet:

- $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
- Acceleration of free fall, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>

Resolve velocity into horizontal and vertical components:

- $v_{h}=25\mathrm{cos}10=24.6ms^{-1}$ **AND**
- $v_{v}=25\mathrm{sin}10=4.34ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the time of the flight:

- $s=ut$
- $s_{h}=v_{h}\timest$
- $t=\frac{30}{24.6}=1.22s$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the vertical displacement after 1.22:

- $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
- $s = \left(4 . 34 \times 1 . 22\right) - \left(\frac{1}{2} \times 9 . 81 \times 1 . 22^{2}\right)$ **[1 mark]**
- Decrease in height = 2.01 m **[1 mark]**

Comment on whether the skier will reach the flat surface before landing:

- The skier's height has decreased by 2.01 m by the time he has travelled a horizontal distance of 30 m
- Therefore he will reach the flat surface before landing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *In this question, upwards is taken as positive*

  - *It doesn't matter which direction you take as positive or negative when using SUVAT equations, as long as it is consistent throughout your question!*
  - *Remember if upwards is taken as positive then **g** will be negative (as it is always directed downwards!)*

parts.problemMd:
Another skier travels along the horizontal surface with an initial speed of 23 m s−1 .

She comes to rest after travelling a distance of 43 m.

Calculate the average force required to bring the skier to rest.

mass of skier = 63 kg

Average force = .............................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average force required to bring the skier to rest:

List the known quantities:

- Initial speed, *u* = 23 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Final speed, *v* = 0
- Distance travelled, *s* = 43 m
- Mass of skier, *m* = 63 kg

Calculate the deceleration of the skier:

- $v^{2}=u^{2}+2as$
- $0 = 23^{2} + \left(2 \times a \times 43\right)$
- $a=\frac{-23^{2}}{86}=-6.15ms^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the force required:

- $ΣF=ma$
- $F=63\times6.15$ **[1 mark]**
- Average force = 387 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
An explosion projects a rock into the air with a speed of 50 m s<sup>–1</sup> at an angle to the horizontal of 40°.

![q16-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/017-q16-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level.png)

Show that the rock would reach its maximum height about 3 s after the explosion.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the rock would reach its maximum height about 3 s after the explosion:

List the known quantities:

- Initial rock velocity, $u$ = 50 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- Angle to horizontal = 40°
- Acceleration of free fall = 9.81 m s<sup>-2</sup>

Determine the vertical component of the initial velocity, $u_{v}$:

- $u_{v} = 50 sin \left(40 \circ\right) = 32 . 1 m s^{- 1}$ **[1 mark]**

List the known and unknown vertical suvat quantities, defining up as the positive direction:

- $s_{v}$ = unknown
- $u_{v}$ = 50sin(40°)
- $v_{v}$ = 0 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- $a$ = −9.81 m s<sup>-2</sup>
- $t$ = to be calculated

Choose a suvat equation and calculate $t$:

- $v=u+at$
- $t = \frac{v - u}{a} = \frac{0 - 50 sin \left(40 \circ\right)}{- 9 . 81}$ **[1 mark]**
- $t=3.28s$
- $\mathrm{time} \mathrm{to} \mathrm{reach} \mathrm{max} \mathrm{height}=3.3s$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *To determine the vertical component of initial velocity, trigonometry is used*

![screenshot-2023-01-13-at-10-22-57](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/018-screenshot-2023-01-13-at-10-22-57.png)

- *For suvat questions, defining your variables clearly is very important*

  - *The acceleration vector points in the **opposite** direction to initial velocity, so they must have **opposite** signs*
  - *This ensures you do not calculate a **negative** value for **time**!*
- *Knowing that the instantaneous final velocity is 0 m s*<sup>*-1*</sup>* when a projectile reaches **maximum** **height** is **crucial** to solving these types of question*

parts.problemMd:
The rock moves in the direction of a hill. The side of the hill is at 20° to the horizontal, as shown.

![q16b-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/019-q16b-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-leve.png)

After a certain distance, the rock lands on the side of the hill.

Deduce whether the rock hits the ground before it reaches its maximum possible height.
parts.solutionMd:
Deduce whether the rock hits the ground before it reaches its maximum possible height:

List the known and unknown vertical suvat quantities to find the maximum height:

- $s_{v,max}$ = to be calculated
- $u_{v}$ = 32.1 m s<sup>-1</sup> (from part **(a)**)
- $v_{v}$ = 0 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- $a$ = −9.81 m s<sup>-2</sup>
- $t_{max}$ = 3.28 s

Use a vertical suvat equation to find maximum height of the projectile:

- $s_{v,max}=u_{v}t_{max}+\frac{1}{2}at_{max}^{2}$
- $s_{v , m a x} = \left(32 . 1 \times 3 . 28\right) - \frac{1}{2} \times 9 . 81 \times \left(3 . 28\right)^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $s_{v,max}=52.5m$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the initial horizontal velocity:

- $u_{h} = 50 cos \left(40 \circ\right) = 38 . 3 m s^{- 1}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the horizontal displacement at $t_{max}$:

- $s_{h,max}=u_{h}t_{max}$
- $s_{h,max}=38.3\times3.28=126m$ **[1 mark]**

Compare the hill height 126 m away with maximum height of the projectile:

- $h = 126 tan \left(20 \circ\right) = 45 . 9 m$**[1 mark]**
- 45.9 m > 52.5 m <u>therefore</u> the answer is no (the rock does not hit the ground before reaching its maximum height); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *You will often find a difficult projectile question like this in your unit 1 paper - make sure it is something you feel confident in!*
- *The key here was to find the location of the projectile at its maximum height and compare that with the location of the hill*

  - *To do this, you had to find vertical **and** horizontal displacement*
  - *Usually, horizontal displacement is found using *$s=ut$*, which is a special case of *$s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$* when acceleration is zero*
- *You may have compared the angle of the hill to the angle of the projectile to the horizontal - this would also have been a valid method*

  - *Sometimes, drawing a diagram is a good way to visualise a complicated scenario such as this one*

![screenshot-2023-01-13-at-11-05-29](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/020-screenshot-2023-01-13-at-11-05-29.png)

parts.problemMd:
A stunt motorcyclist wants to jump across a river to land on the other side. The diagram shows the motorcyclist driving off a ramp at the edge of a river.

![q18-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/028-q18-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy.png)

The ramp is at an angle of 25° to the horizontal and the height at the end of the ramp is 3.0 m. The width of the river is 100 m. The initial velocity of the motorcyclist is 35 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the motorcycle's initial velocity as it leaves the ramp.

Horizontal component = ......................

Vertical component = ......................
parts.solutionMd:
Use trigonometry to resolve the horizontal and vertical components of velocity:

![vector-trig](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/029-vector-trig.png)

- Resolving horizontally (→): *v*<sub>*x*</sub> = 35 × cos 25° = 31.7 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Resolving vertically (↑): *v*<sub>*y*</sub> = 35 × sin 25° = 14.8 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Horizontal component = 32 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**
- Vertical component = 15 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Deduce whether the rider lands on the other side of the river.

The effects of air resistance can be ignored.
parts.solutionMd:
Deduce whether the rider lands on the other side of the river:

List the known quantities:

- Required horizontal distance, *s* = 100 m
- Vertical height above ground, *h* = 3.00 m
- Horizontal initial velocity, *u*<sub>*x*</sub> = 31.7 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Vertical initial velocity, *u*<sub>*y*</sub> = 14.8 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Horizontal acceleration, *a*<sub>*x*</sub> = 0
- Vertical acceleration, *a*<sub>*y*</sub> = −*g* = −9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>

Max **four** marks from **one** of the following methods:

**Method 1: Comparison of vertical distances**

Determine the time taken to travel 100 m horizontally:

- $s=u_{x}t$
- $t=\frac{100}{31.7}$ = 3.155 s **[1 mark]**

Determine the vertical distance fallen in this time:

- $s=u_{y}t+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
- $s = \left(14 . 8 \times 3 . 155\right) - \frac{1}{2} \times \left(9 . 81 \times 3 . 155^{2}\right)$ = −2.13 m **[1 mark]**
- Vertical distance fallen = 2.1 m **[1 mark]**

Write a concluding statement:

- When the rider has travelled 100 m horizontally, they have fallen a distance of 2.1 m which is less than 3.0 m, hence the rider lands on the other side of the river; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

**Method 2: Comparison of times of flight**

Determine the time to the maximum height:

- $v=u_{y}+at$
- $0=14.8-9.81t\Rightarrowt=\frac{14.8}{9.81}=1.5s$

Solve the quadratic to determine the time to descend by 3 m:

- $s=u_{y}t+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
- $3 . 0 = 14 . 8 t - \frac{9 . 81}{2} t^{2} \Rightarrow t = \frac{14 . 8 - \sqrt{14 . 8^{2} - \left(2 \times 9 . 81 \times 3\right)}}{9 . 81} = 0 . 22 s$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the total time of flight of the rider:

- Time of flight = (2 × time to reach max height) + (time to descend 3 m)
- Time of flight = (2 × 1.5) + 0.22
- Time of flight = 3.22 s **[1 mark]**

Determine the horizontal distance travelled in this time:

- $s=u_{x}t=31.7\times3.22=102.1m$
- Horizontal distance travelled = 102 m **[1 mark]**

Write a concluding statement:

- The rider travels a total horizontal distance of 102 m which is greater than 100 m, hence the rider lands on the other side of the river; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

**Method 3: Comparison of horizontal distances**

Determine the time taken to travel 100 m horizontally (as in **Method 1**):

- Time to travel 100 m horizontally = 3.16 s **[1 mark]**

Determine the time of flight (as in **Method 2**):

- Time to descend by 3 m = 0.22 s **[1 mark]**
- Time of flight = 3.22 s **[1 mark]**

Write a concluding statement:

- It takes the rider 3.16 s to travel 100 m horizontally which is less than 3.22 s, the total time of flight, hence the rider lands on the other side of the river; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Method 1** is by far the simplest way to tackle this question as this requires the fewest calculation steps and no quadratic formula*

  - *The other two methods give equally clear results but are more prone to calculation errors along the way*

- *For example, a very common error made in **Method 2** tends to be calculating the time to reach the greatest height and then doubling it but forgetting to include the time taken to fall the last 3.00 m*
- *This is why drawing a clear sketch can be very helpful to avoid this type of mistake:*

![projectile-sketch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/030-projectile-sketch.png)

- *Calculation errors are common when students are unsure about how to carry out the quadratic step in **Method 2*
- *The full working of this step is shown below:*

![quadratic-projectile-calculation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/031-quadratic-projectile-calculation.png)

parts.problemMd: Explain how air resistance would affect the jump.
parts.solutionMd:
The effect of air resistance on the rider's motion would be:

- Air resistance acts to oppose the motion of the motorcyclist; **[1 mark]**

Max **one** from:

- It decreases the time for which the motorcyclist is in the air; **[1 mark]**
- It causes deceleration in the horizontal direction; **[1 mark]**
- It reduces speed in the horizontal direction; **[1 mark]**
- It reduces the (maximum) height reached by the motorcyclist; **[1 mark]**

If any mark is gained from the above, max **one** for:

- It reduces the horizontal distance travelled; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You could also use a diagram to aid your description - a clearly annotated sketch could earn you some marks*

![projectile-air-resistance](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/motion/assets/032-projectile-air-resistance.png)

parts.problemMd:
During a test run, the train accelerates uniformly from rest to a maximum speed of $505\text{km h}^{-1}$ and maintains this speed for $130\text{s}$. The train decelerates uniformly at the same rate and completes the test in a total time of $480\text{s}$.

Calculate the average speed of the train during the test run.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average speed of the train:

- List the known quantities:

  - Maximum speed, $v_{max}=505\text{km h}^{-1}$
  - Total time at max speed, $t_{max}=130\text{s}$
  - Total time of test, $T=480\text{s}$

- Convert the maximum speed to $\text{m s}^{-1}$:

$v_{max}=\frac{505\times1000}{3600}=140.3\text{m s}^{-1}$

- Determine the total distance travelled by the train:

  - Since the rates of acceleration and deceleration are the same, the velocity–time graph would be a trapezium
  - Area of trapezium $= \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$

$s=\frac{1}{2}(t_{max}+T)v_{max}$

$s=\frac{1}{2}(130+480)\times140.3$

$s=42790\text{m}$ **[1 mark]**

- Determine the average speed of the train:

$v_{av}=\frac{s}{T}$

$v_{av}=\frac{42790}{480}$ **[1 mark]**

$v_{av}=$ $89.1\text{m s}^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating the total distance travelled
> 
> - Accept any valid method, e.g. using the area under the speed–time graph or kinematic equations
> 
> 1 mark for use of $v_{av}=s/t$ with $t=480\text{s}$
> 
> 1 mark for a final answer of $89\text{m s}^{-1}$ (or $320\text{km h}^{-1}$)

parts.problemMd:
The Tyrolean traverse is a technique for crossing a deep valley. The photograph shows a climber crossing a river using this technique. The climber moves along a rope suspended from the bank on either side of the river.

![q13-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/007-q13-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy.png)

The free-body force diagram for the climber is shown below. The weight of the climber is 650 N.

![q13a-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/008-q13a-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-ph.png)

Show that the tension *T* in the rope is about 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> N.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the tension *T* in the rope is about 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> N:

![file-000---2023-01-13t155501-419](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/009-file-000-2023-01-13t155501-419.png)

- Use trignometry to resolve *T* vertically:  $\mathrm{cos}θ=\frac{adj}{hyp}=\frac{T_{v}}{T}$
- Resolving *T* vertically:  $T_{v} = T cos \left(76 \circ\right)$** [1 mark]**
- When the forces are in equilibrium, Upward forces = Downward forces
- Hence, $W = 2 T_{v} = 2 T cos \left(76 \circ\right)$

Calculate the tension *T*:

- $T = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{W}{cos \left(76 \circ\right)} = \frac{650}{2 \times cos \left(76 \circ\right)}$ **[1 mark]**
- $T=1343N$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The rope has an unstretched length of 120 m as shown below.

![q13b-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/010-q13b-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-ph.png)

i) Determine the strain in the rope while it is supporting the weight of the climber.

You may ignore the weight of the rope.

Strain = ..................................**(3)**

ii) The rope has a cross-sectional area of 3.14 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>

Determine the Young modulus of the rope material.

Young modulus = ..................................**(3)**
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Original length of rope, $x$ = 120 m
- Tension in rope, *T* = 1343 N
- Cross-sectional area of rope, *A* = 3.14 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>

i) Determine the strain in the rope while it is supporting the weight of the climber:

![file-000---2023-01-13t165829-653](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/011-file-000-2023-01-13t165829-653.png)

- Using trigonometry:  $\frac{1}{2} \left(x + \Delta x\right) = \frac{ 60}{sin \left(76 \circ\right)} = 61 . 8 m$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the extension:

- $x + \Delta x = 2 \times 61 . 8 \Rightarrow \Delta x = \left(2 \times 61 . 8\right) - x$
- $\Delta x = \left(2 \times 61 . 8\right) - 120 = 3 . 7 m$

Determine the strain:

- Strain:  $ε=\frac{\Deltax}{x}=\frac{3.7}{120}=0.031$ **[1 mark]**
- $ε$ = 0.03 **or** 3% **[1 mark]**

ii) Determine the Young modulus of the rope material:

- Stress:  $σ=\frac{F}{A}=\frac{1343}{3.14\times10^{-4}}=4.28\times10^{6}\mathrm{Pa}$ **[1 mark]**
- Young Modulus:  $E=\frac{σ}{ε}=\frac{4.28\times10^{6}}{0.031}=1.38\times10^{8}\mathrm{Pa}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E = 1 . 4 \times 10^{8} Pa \left(2 s . f .\right)$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *For part (ii) remember that the force is the tension calculated in part (a)*

parts.problemMd:
A pulley system is used to lift a 5.00 kN load through a height of 1.50 m. The system consists of one fixed pulley and the other pulley can move. The pulleys are connected by a nylon rope, as shown.

![q17-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/006-q17-wph11-01-june-2021-edexcel-int-as-a-level-ph.png)

The nylon rope will stretch when it is used in this way. The weight of the pulleys and the rope can be ignored, and you may assume that there is no friction in the pulleys.

The properties of the nylon rope are:

| Young modulus of nylon | 2.70 GPa |
|---|---|
| overall length of rope before adding the load | 6.00 m |
| area of cross-section | 3.00 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> |

The greater the length of a rope, the smaller the stiffness of the rope.

Explain why.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain why the greater the length of a rope, the smaller the stiffness of the rope:

- The greater the length of the rope, the greater the extension ($\Deltax$) for a given force; **[1 mark]**
- Stiffness $k=\frac{F}{\Deltax}$ therefore stiffness decreases (if extension increases);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
i) Show that the stiffness k of the nylon rope is about 1.4 × 10<sup>5</sup> N m<sup>−1</sup> .

**(3)**

ii) The pulley system lifts the 5.00 kN weight at a steady rate.

Determine the extension of the rope while the lift is taking place.

Extension of rope = ............................**(3)**

iii) Calculate the work done in stretching the rope.

Work done in stretching rope = ..........................**(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) Show that the stiffness *k* of the nylon rope is about 1.4 × 10<sup>5</sup> N m<sup>−1</sup>:

List the known quantities:

- Young modulus of nylon, *E *= 2.70 GPa = 2.70 × 10<sup>9</sup> Pa
- Overall length of rope before adding the load = 6.00 m
- Area of cross-section, *A* = 3.00 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>

Determine an equation for the young modulus, *E *and substitute in the values:

- $E=\frac{σ}{ε}$, $σ=\frac{F}{A}$ and $ε=\frac{\Deltax}{x}$
- $E = \frac{\left(\frac{F}{A}\right)}{\left(\frac{\Delta x}{x}\right)} = \frac{F x}{A \Delta x}$ **[1 mark]**

Write the equation in terms of *k*:

- $F=k\Deltax$
- $E=\frac{k\Deltax\timesx}{A\Deltax}=\frac{kx}{A}$

Rearrange for *k* and substitute in the values:

- $k = \frac{ E A}{x} = \frac{\left(2 . 70 \times 10^{9}\right) \times \left(3 . 00 \times 10^{4}\right)}{6 . 00}$ **[1 mark]**
- $k=1.35\times10^{5}Nm^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

ii) Determine the extension of the rope while the lift is taking place:

List the known quantities:

- Weight, *W* = 5.00 kN = 5000 N

Determine the tension in the rope, *T*:

- Tension in the rope is constant, therefore the tension on each side is half the weight
- $T=\frac{W}{2}=\frac{5000}{2}=2500N$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the extension of the rope, Δx:

- $\Deltax=\frac{F}{k}=\frac{2500}{1.35\times105}$ **[1 mark]**
- Extension of rope = 1.85 × 10<sup>−2</sup> m **[1 mark]**

iii) Calculate the work done in stretching the rope:

- $\Delta E_{e l} = \frac{1}{2} F \Delta x = \frac{1}{2} \times 2500 \times \left(1 . 85 \times 10^{- 2}\right)$ **[1 mark]**
- Work done = 23.13 J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *The work done is the **energy transferred**, in this case, it is the **elastic potential energy*

parts.problemMd: Assess whether the stretching of the rope has a significant effect on the efficiency of the pulley system.
parts.solutionMd:
Assess whether the stretching of the rope has a significant effect on the efficiency of the pulley system:

List the known quantities:

- Weight of the load, $F$ = 5000 N
- Distance moved, $\Deltas$= 1.5 m

Find the work done in lifting the load:

- $W=F\Deltas=5000\times1.5=7500J$ **[1 mark]**

Compare with the work done in stretching the rope:

- 23.1 J is much smaller than 7500 J therefore there is no significant effect; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *For the second mark you must write a **concluding** sentence, don't just leave your answer at the calculation!*

parts.problemMd:
A student carried out an experiment to determine the Young modulus of a sample of stainless steel in the form of a wire. The student added weights to the wire and measured the corresponding extensions.

The wire had an unstretched length of 2.6 m. The diameter of the wire was 5.6 × 10<sup>–4 </sup>m.

The student plotted a graph of weight against extension. The graph showed that the limit of proportionality was not exceeded.

State what is meant by the limit of proportionality.
parts.solutionMd:
State what is meant by the limit of proportionality:

Any **one** from:

- Maximum value of weight / force for which weight / force is proportional to extension; **[1 mark]**
- Point beyond which Hooke's Law no longer applies; **[1 mark]**
- Point beyond which weight/force is no longer proportional to extension; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *"Point beyond which graph line ceases to be straight" would have gained a mark here in an exam, but less specific language like this does not always guarantee a mark*

  - *It is best to be sure and use **specific** physics language - for example "the point at which a force-extension graph line ceases to be straight" is much better*

parts.problemMd:
The student's graph is shown below.

![q14b-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/004-q14b-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-leve.png)

i) Determine the gradient of the graph. ** **

Gradient = ................................................**(2)**

ii) Determine the Young modulus of stainless steel using your value for the gradient.

** **Young modulus = ........................................**(3)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) Determine the gradient of the graph:

Use a triangle on the graph to determine the gradient:

![screenshot-2023-01-12-at-16-57-55](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/005-screenshot-2023-01-12-at-16-57-55.png)

- <u>Large</u> (Δ*x* > 1.5) triangle to determine gradient; **[1 mark]**

Calculate gradient:

- $gradient = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{39 - 0}{\left(2 . 1 \times 10^{- 3}\right) - 0} = 18 570 = 18 600 N m^{- 1}$
- $\mathrm{gradient}=19000Nm^{-1}$ (accepted answers round to 18 000 or 19 000 to 2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

ii) Determine the Young modulus of stainless steel using your value for the gradient:

List the known quantities:

- gradient of weight vs extension, $k$ = 18 600 N m<sup>-1</sup>
- Unstretched wire length, $x$ = 2.6 m
- Wire diameter, $d$ = 5.6 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m

From the list of data, formulae and relationships:

- $E=\frac{σ}{ε}$ (Young's modulus)
- $σ=\frac{F}{A}$ (stress)
- $ε=\frac{Δx}{x}$ (strain)

Substitute the equations for stress and strain into the equation for Young's modulus:

- $E = \frac{F/A}{\left(\Delta x\right)/x} = \frac{F x}{\left(\Delta x\right) A}$

Substitute the gradient from part **(i)**:

- $k=\frac{ΔF}{Δx}$
- $Ε=\frac{kx}{A}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the cross-sectional area:

- $A = \pi r^{2} = \pi \left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}$
- $A = \frac{\pi \times \left(5 . 6 \times 10^{- 4}\right)^{2}}{4} = 2 . 46 \times 10^{- 7} m^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate $E$ using this:

- $\mathbf{E} = \frac{k x}{A} = \frac{\left(18 600\right) \times 2 . 6}{\left(2 . 46 \times 10^{- 7}\right)} = 1 . 963 \times 10^{11} Pa$
- $\mathrm{Young}'s\mathrm{modulus}=2.0\times10^{11}\mathrm{Pa}$ (range of 1.9 to 2.0 × 10<sup>11</sup> Pa accepted) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *When calculating a gradient, make the triangle as **large** as possible*
- *Use values at points where the graph crosses through grid lines - this takes the guesswork out of trying to figure out whether the point of the graph is "halfway" up a small box or "0.6" of the way up it*

parts.problemMd:
The breaking stress for this stainless steel is known to be 480 MPa.

Deduce whether it is safe for the student to increase the weight to 100.0 N.
parts.solutionMd:
Deduce whether it is safe for the student to increase the weight to 100.0 N:

List the known quantities:

- Cross-sectional area of wire, $A$ = 2.46 × 10<sup>-7</sup> m<sup>2</sup>
- Breaking stress, $σ_{max}$ = 480 MPa = 4.80 × 10<sup>8</sup> Pa

Use the stress equation to determine the maximum force:

- $σ_{max}=\frac{F_{max}}{A}$
- $F_{m a x} = A \sigma_{m a x} = \left(2 . 46 \times 10^{- 7}\right) \times \left(4 . 80 \times 10^{8}\right)$ **[1 mark]**
- $\mathrm{max} \mathrm{force}=118N$ **[1 mark]**

Compare this to the student's proposed added weight:

- 118 N is greater than 100 N <u>therefore</u> it is safe; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Alternatively, you could have calculated the stress caused by 100.0 N and determined whether it was below the breaking stress of 480 MPa*

parts.problemMd:
*The photograph shows a toy car that contains a spring. Pulling the car backwards along the floor compresses the spring. Energy is stored in the compressed spring.

![q15-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/003-q15-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level.png)

The car is released and the spring returns to its original state. There is a forward force on the car from the floor and the car moves forwards.

Explain why the floor exerts a forward force on the car and how this force affects the motion of the car as the spring returns to its original state.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain why the floor exerts a forward force on the car and how this force affects the motion of the car as the spring returns to its original state:

The following list is the 'indicative marking points'. Stating all six will score four marks, less than six is marked according to a scale given below. The remaining two marks are given for the linking and explanation:

*Indicative Content (IC):*

1. There is a (backward) force / friction on floor from wheels / car
2. Newton's Third Law implies forward / opposite force from floor
3. Compression / deformation of spring reduces (as car moves forward)
4. (Resultant) force is proportional to compression / deformation of spring **OR **reference to Hooke's Law
5. Acceleration is proportional to resultant force **OR** reference to $F=ma$
6. Acceleration reduces (as distance travelled increases) **OR** acceleration becomes zero once spring returns to original state

**An example answer which scores six marks is:**

As the wheels rotate, there is a backward friction force on the floor from the wheels **[1]**. As a result of this, **[linkage]** the floor exerts an equal and opposite forward force on the wheels, implied by Newton's third law **[2]**. The spring's compression decreases **[3]**** **as the car moves and that compression is proportional to the forward force, according to $ΔF=kΔx$ **[4]**. Acceleration is proportional to this resultant force **[5]**, therefore **[linkage] **acceleration reduces to zero as the spring returns to its original state **[6]**.

- Six indicative marking points; **[4 marks]**
- Linkage made between forward and backward force **AND** link between reducing spring compression and reducing acceleration; **[2 marks]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *The starred written questions assess your ability to **link** **facts** in a logically **structured** answer.*
- *In the table below, **indicative content (IC) points** are form the list above. The second column shows the **maximum marks** you can earn from these **statements**.*

  - *As you see, **6** correct **statements** are worth a total of **4 marks**.*
- *The third column is for ‘**linkage marks**’. This means how well you linked the statements in your argument. The maximum linkage mark depends on the number of statements. *

  - *Even if you linked well, only **one** linkage mark is available if you only mentioned **4 out of 6** IC points*
- *To score 6/6 marks, you will need a **full** **paragraph**, using a "point, evidence, explain" structure, **as well as** using your Physics to link together at least six points from the content you have learned. *

| > *IC points* | > *IC mark* | > *Maximum linkage marks available* | > *Maximum final mark* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *6* | > *4* | > *2* | > *6* |
| > *5* | > *3* | > *2* | > *5* |
| > *4* | > *3* | > *1* | > *4* |
| > *3* | > *2* | > *1* | > *3* |
| > *2* | > *2* | > *0* | > *2* |
| > *1* | > *1* | > *0* | > *1* |
| > *0* | > *0* | > *0* | > *0* |

parts.problemMd:
The photograph shows a toy pinball machine. The launcher is pulled back, compressing a spring. The spring obeys Hooke’s law. When the launcher is released, the spring returns to its original length and a small ball is launched horizontally into the machine.

![q16-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/012-q16-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy.png)

When the launcher is pulled back, the spring is compressed by 5.0 cm. When the spring is released, the ball is launched at a speed of 8.0 cm s<sup>−1</sup>.

Show that the kinetic energy of the ball just after launching is about 4 × 10<sup>−5</sup> J.

mass of ball = 12 g
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the kinetic energy of the ball just after launching is about 4 × 10<sup>−5</sup> J:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of ball, *m* = 12 g = 12 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg
- Speed of launch, *v* = 8.0 cm s<sup>−1</sup> = 8.0 × 10<sup>−2</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the kinetic energy:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- $E_{k} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(12 \times 10^{- 3}\right) \times \left(8 . 0 \times 10^{- 2}\right)^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = 3.84 × 10<sup>−5</sup> J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Determine the force on the ball when the spring is released.

Force = ................................
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the force on the ball when the spring is released:

List the known quantities:

- Kinetic energy after launch, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = 3.84 × 10<sup>−5</sup> J
- Spring compression, Δ*x *= 5.0 cm = 0.05 m

Since the elastic energy stored in the spring is equal to the kinetic energy after launch:

- $\DeltaE_{el}=\frac{1}{2}F\Deltax$
- $\DeltaE_{el}=\frac{1}{2}\timesF\times0.05=3.84\times10^{-5}J$ **[1 mark]**
- $F = \frac{2 \times \left(3 . 84 \times 10^{- 5}\right)}{0 . 05}$
- *F* = 1.54 × 10<sup>−3</sup> N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Determine the stiffness of the spring.

Stiffness = ..............................
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the stiffness of the spring:

- Hooke's Law:  $F=k\Deltax$
- $1.54\times10^{-3}=k\times0.05$ **[1 mark]**
- $k=\frac{1.54\times10^{-3}}{0.05}$ = 0.0308
- Stiffness = 0.031 N m<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The spring returns to its original length* L*.

Sketch a graph, on the axes below, to show how the velocity of the ball varies with the length of the spring.

![q16d-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/013-q16d-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-ph.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The graph showing the variation of launch velocity with the length of the spring is as follows:

![velocity-length-graph](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/stretching-materials/assets/014-velocity-length-graph.png)

- Line has initially decreasing positive gradient; **[1 mark]**
- Line starts at *v* = 0 and a non-zero value of length; **[1 mark]**
- Line levels off to horizontal at length = *L*; **[1 mark]**
- Final velocity marked as 8.0 cm s<sup>−1</sup> **or** original compressed length marked as (*L* − 5) in cm; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *If you look at this and think this is a difficult graph drawing question, then you're right, not many students could get this one in the exam!*
- *Here, it's worth taking some time to think about the situation given:*

- *At the point at which the spring is released from maximum compression:*

  - *The ball is initially at rest, so **v** = 0 when length = (**L **− 5) cm*
  - *The spring cannot have a length of 0, therefore, the graph should not go through the origin*

- *At the point the ball is launched, the spring reaches its original length:*

  - *The ball has a launch velocity of **v** = 8 cm s*<sup>*−1*</sup>* when length = **L*

- *Then, the hard part is considering how **v** will vary between (**L **− 5) and **L:*

  - *If the acceleration was constant, then the gradient would be constant*
  - *However, considering the relationship between force and extension (**F** = **k**Δ**x**) and Newton's second law (**F** = **ma**), the acceleration is **not** going to be constant*

> *Since  **F** ∝ Δ**x**  and  **F** ∝ **a** *

> *And ** E*<sub>*el*</sub>* ∝ **E*<sub>*k*</sub>*  *

> *This means  **F** ∝ **v*<sup>*2*</sup>

> *∴** a **∝** v*<sup>*2*</sup>* ∝ Δ**x*

- *This means that a graph of **v*<sup>*2*</sup>* against length would give a straight line, but **v** against length will not*

  - *For large compressions, the gradient will be** larger** than at small compressions*
  - *Hence, the gradient will **decrease** as the length is increased*

parts.problemMd:
A toy car is released from rest and rolls down a slope, as shown.

![q11-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/work-energy-and-power/assets/004-q11-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level.png)

mass of car = 0.160 kg

speed of car at bottom of slope = 2.6 m s<sup>–1</sup>.

Calculate the increase in kinetic energy of the car as it accelerates down the slope.

Increase in kinetic energy = .......................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the increase in kinetic energy of the car as it accelerates down the slope:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of car, $m$ = 0.160 kg
- Speed of car at bottom of slope, $v$ = 2.6 m s<sup>–1</sup>

Substitute the known quantities into the equation for kinetic energy:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}\times0.160\times2.6^{2}=0.541J$ **[1 mark]**
- Increase in kinetic energy = 0.54 J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Increase in kinetic energy is final KE - initial KE*

  - *The initial KE is zero as the car is at rest, so increase in KE = final KE*

parts.problemMd:
As the car accelerates down the slope, the work done against frictional forces is 0.26 J.

Calculate the vertical displacement of the car.

Vertical displacement of car = ...................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the vertical displacement of the car:

List the known quantities:

- Work done against frictional forces, $ΔW$ = 0.26 J
- Increase in kinetic energy, $ΔE_{k}$ = 0.54 J (from part (a))
- Mass of car, $m$ = 0.16 kg
- Acceleration of free fall, $g$ = 9.81 m s<sup>-2</sup>

Use the conservation of energy:

- Loss in gravitational potential energy = $ΔW$ + $ΔE_{k}$

Substitute in the equation for GPE and rearrange for displacement:

- $mgΔh=ΔW+ΔE_{k}$
- $Δh=\frac{ΔW+ΔE_{k}}{mg}=\frac{0.26+0.54}{0.16\times9.81}=0.510m$ **[1 mark]**
- $\mathrm{vertical} \mathrm{displacement}=0.51m$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The car starts off with energy **only** in its gravitational potential store*

  - *This is all the car has to "spend"*
  - *This energy is transferred into an internal store (friction) and kinetic store and nowhere else*
  - *The sum of energy in these stores is equal to the initial energy in the GPE store*

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a lift system for moving people up and down a tall building. There is a counterweight to balance the weight of the lift. An electric motor is used to raise and lower the lift.

![q12-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/work-energy-and-power/assets/005-q12-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy.png)

Explain how the counterweight affects the amount of work required from the electric motor to raise the lift.
parts.solutionMd:
When the lift is going up, the counterweight:

- Reduces / decreases the amount of work done by the motor; **[1 mark]**
- Because the counterweight reduces the force required from the motor; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *For the second marking point, you could also have said:*

  - *Because there is energy transferred between the counterweight and the lift*
  - *Because the counterweight contributes to the total work done (on the lift cage)*
  - *Because the total work done (on the lift cage) is the sum of the work done by the counterweight / gravity and by the motor*

- *Remember that work done is the same thing as the amount of energy transferred during a process*
- *Examiners reported that this question was generally answered poorly as students failed to use force or energy in their explanations*

  - *Make sure you understand how force and energy are related in terms of work done (1 N m = 1 J)*

parts.problemMd:
The electric motor raises the lift through a height of 40.0 m in a time of 30.0 s.

Show that the output power of the electric motor is about 12 kW.

total mass of lift and people = 2250 kg

mass of counterweight = 1300 kg
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the output power of the electric motor is about 12 kW:

List the known quantities:

- Height raised, $\Deltah$ = 40.0 m
- Time, $\Deltat$ = 30.0 s
- Total mass of lift and people = 2250 kg
- Mass of counterweight = 1300 kg

**EITHER**

**Method 1: Using conservation of energy**

- GPE: $\DeltaE_{grav}=mg\Deltah$
- For the lift: $\DeltaE_{grav}=2250\times9.81\times40.0=8.829\times10^{5}J$ **AND**
- For the counterweight: $\DeltaE_{grav}=1300\times9.81\times40.0=5.101\times10^{5}J$ **[1 mark]**
- $\Delta W = \left(8 . 829 \times 10^{5}\right) - \left(5 . 101 \times 10^{5}\right) = 3 . 728 \times 10^{5} J$ **[1 mark]**

**OR**

**Method 2: Using resultant force**

- Weight: $F=mg$ and Work done: $\DeltaW=F\Deltax$
- Weight of lift: $F=2250\timesg$
- Weight of counterweight: $F=1300\timesg$
- $\Delta F = \left(2250 - 1300\right) \times g = 950 \times g$ **[1 mark]**
- $\DeltaW=950\times9.81\times40.0=3.728\times10^{5}J$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total power output:

- $P=\frac{\DeltaW}{\Deltat}$
- $P=\frac{3.728\times10^{5}}{30}$ **[1 mark]**
- $P = 1 . 243 \times 10^{4} W = 12 . 4 kW \left(3 s . f .\right)$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The electric motor dissipates energy to the surroundings at a rate of 3600 W.

Determine the efficiency of the electric motor.

Efficiency = .............................
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the efficiency of the electric motor:

- Efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input
- Efficiency $=\frac{12400}{12400+3600}$ **[1 mark]**
- Efficiency $= 0 . 78 \left(2 s . f .\right)$**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The key to answering this question correctly is recognising that the total power input is the power used by the motor plus the rate of energy transferred (wastefully) to the surroundings*

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a system used to move a stone block up a ramp. A team of people uses a rope to pull the block at a constant speed.

![q18-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/work-energy-and-power/assets/006-q18-wph11-01-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level.png)

height of ramp = 4.35 m

angle of ramp to horizontal = 6.0°

mass of block = 2.10 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg

speed of block up ramp = 0.450 m s<sup>–1</sup>

total power of team = 6.25 kW

Show that the total force that the team exerts on the block is about 14 kN.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the total force that the team exerts on the block is about 14 kN:

List the known quantities:

- Speed of the block, $v$ = 0.450 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- Power of team, $P$ = 6.25 kW = 6250 W

Determine the work done each second using the power equation:

- $P=\frac{W}{t}$
- In 1 second, 6250 J are transferred

Use the speed equation to determine displacement each second:

- $v=\frac{Δs}{Δt}$
- In 1 second, the block is displaced 0.450 m

Use the work done equation to calculate force:

- $ΔW=FΔs$
- $F=\frac{ΔW}{Δs}=\frac{6250}{0.450}$ **[1 mark]**
- $F=13900N=13.9\mathrm{kN}$ (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *A more concise way of performing this calculation is to divide both sides of the work done equation by change in time*

$ΔW=FΔs$

$\frac{ΔW}{Δt}=F\frac{Δs}{Δt}$

- *By spotting the rate of work done on the rate and the rate of displacement on the right, the equation becomes:*

$P=Fv$

- *Both methods are doing the exact same thing - see which works best for you!*

parts.problemMd:
Determine the total work done by the team.

Total work done = ...........................................
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the total work done by the team:

List the known quantities:

- Height of ramp = 4.35 m
- Angle of ramp = 6.0°
- Force applied, $F$ = 13.9 kN = 13.9 × 10<sup>3</sup> N

Calculate the displacement $Δs$ of the block:

- The displacement is the length of the ramp
- $\Delta s = \frac{4 . 35}{sin \left(6 . 0 \circ\right)} = 41 . 62 m$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for work done:

- $\Delta W = F \Delta s = \left(13 . 9 \times 10^{3}\right) \times 41 . 62$ **[1 mark]**
- $ΔW=578500J$
- $\mathrm{Total} \mathrm{work} \mathrm{done}=5.8\times10^{5}J$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Show that the useful work done on the block is about 90 kJ.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the useful work done on the block is about 90 kJ:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the block, $m$ = 2.10 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg
- Height of the ramp, $h$ = 4.35 m
- Acceleration of free fall, $g$ = 9.81 m s<sup>-2</sup>

Determine the useful work done:

- Useful work = gain in energy in gravitational potential store
- $\Delta E_{g r a v} = m g \Delta h = \left(2 . 10 \times 10^{3}\right) \times 9 . 81 \times 4 . 35$ **[1 mark]**
- $ΔE_{grav}=89610J$
- $\mathrm{Useful} \mathrm{work}=89.6\mathrm{kJ}$ (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The team's objective in this question is to pull to block **up** the ramp*

  - *The useful work done is spent raising the block's height - this work is done against gravity and is equal to the energy gain in the gravitational potential store*
- *Here, the answer must be given to **three significant figures*

  - *All the information used to answer the question is given to three significant figures, and the answer must have the same number of significant figures as the **least precise given value*
  - *An example of this is given below*

![a-sigfig-example](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/work-energy-and-power/assets/007-a-sigfig-example.png)

parts.problemMd:
Determine the efficiency of the system.

Efficiency = ........................................
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the efficiency of the system:

List the known quantities:

- Total work done = 578 × 10<sup>3</sup> J (from part **(b)**)
- Useful work done = 89.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> J (from part **(c)**)

Determine the efficiency of the system:

- $efficiency=\frac{usefulenergyoutput}{totalenergyinput}=\frac{89.6\times10^{3}}{578\times10^{3}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\mathrm{Efficiency}=0.155=0.16$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A cyclist rides up a hill of gradient 1 in 3, as shown. The total mass of the cyclist and bicycle is $75  \text{kg}$.

![Side view of a cyclist on a straight inclined road. The road rises from left to right with horizontal length labelled 3.0 metres and vertical height labelled 1.0 metres.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/1-mechanics-and-materials/work-energy-and-power/assets/003-side-view-of-a-cyclist-on-a-straight-inclined-ro.png)

Show that the component of the total weight parallel to the slope is approximately $230  \text{N}$.
parts.solutionMd:
To show that the component of the total weight parallel to the slope is approximately $230  \text{N}$:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass of cyclist and bicycle, $m = 75  \text{kg}$
  - Vertical height of the slope, $a=1.0\text{m}$
  - Horizontal length of the slope, $b = 3 . 0  \text{m}$
  - Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 9 . 81  \text{m s}^{-2}$
- Use Pythagoras' theorem to find the slope length:

$L=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\sqrt{1.0^{2}+3.0^{2}}=\sqrt{10}\text{m}$

- Use trigonometry to find $\mathrm{sin}θ$:

$\mathrm{sin}θ=\frac{a}{L}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$

- The component of weight parallel to the slope is:

$W_{\parallel} = m g sin \theta$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute and evaluate the answer:

$W_{\parallel} = m g \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$

$W_{\parallel} = 75 \times 9 . 81 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} = 232 . 6 \text{N} \approx 230 \text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for resolving the weight parallel to the slope as $mg\mathrm{sin}θ$
> 
> - Accept $75g\mathrm{sin}θ$ or $735\mathrm{sin}θ$ or $735.8\mathrm{sin}θ$ or $735.75\mathrm{sin}θ$
> - Accept $\mathrm{sin}18.4^{\circ}$ or use of $θ=\mathrm{tan}^{-1}(1/3)$
> - Do not accept $W\mathrm{sin}θ$ unless $W$ is defined as $mg$
> 
> 1 mark for obtaining an answer that rounds to $230\text{N}$
> 
> - Must be quoted to at least 3 significant figures

> **[exam-tip]**
> A "1 in 3" gradient means the road rises $1  \text{m}$ for every $3  \text{m}$ of horizontal distance, so $\mathrm{tan}θ=\frac{1}{3}$, *not* $\mathrm{sin}θ=\frac{1}{3}$. For "show that" questions, always give your answer to one significant figure more than the stated value — writing only "$230  \text{N}$" would lose the final mark even with correct physics.

parts.problemMd:
The cyclist moves with a constant velocity of $2.2\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Calculate the total power output of the cyclist.

resistive force on the cyclist = $25\text{N}$
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the cyclist's total power output:

- List the known quantities:

  - Parallel component of weight, `W_{\parallel} = 232.6 \textrm{ }\text{N}` (from part a)
  - Resistive force, $F_{R} = 25  \text{N}$
  - Velocity along the slope, $v = 2 . 2  \text{m s}^{-1}$
- Determine the total force along the slope

  - At constant velocity, the resultant force is zero, so the total (driving) force balances the parallel component of weight plus the resistive force

$F = W_{\parallel} + F_{R}$

$F=232.6+25=257.6\text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total power:

$P=\frac{W}{t}=\frac{F\Deltas}{t}=Fv$

$P=257.6\times2.2$ **[1 mark]**

$P=$ $567\text{W}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for finding the total force along the slope ($F = W_{\parallel} + F_{R}$)
> 
> - Allow ecf from part (a) if an incorrect value of $W_{\parallel}$ is used
> 
> 1 mark for substitution into $\DeltaW=F\Deltas$ and $P=W/t$ (or $P=Fv$)
> 
> - Accept any equivalent energy/work route (e.g. vertical height gained per second and $\DeltaW=mg\Deltah$)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $567  \text{W}$
> 
> - Accept answers in range $560$–$570\text{W}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> At constant velocity the cyclist's driving force balances *both* the parallel weight component and the resistive force — omitting either is the most common slip on this style of question. The total power output is the rate at which the driving force does work on the bike: $P = F_{\text{drive}} \times v$. The *useful* power (rate of gain of GPE) would be only `W_{\parallel} \times v \approx 510 \textrm{ }\text{W}`; the rest is dissipated against air resistance and friction at the contact surfaces.

parts.problemMd: Which of the following units is equivalent to the volt?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Volts are equivalent to energy transferred (or work done) per unit charge
- $V=\frac{W}{Q}$
- Therefore, the units are J C<sup>−1</sup>

  - This is answer option **C**

parts.problemMd:
The graph shows how potential difference $V$ varies with current $I$ for an electrical component.

![q1-wph12-02-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/2-waves-and-electricity/current-potential-difference-resistance-and-power/assets/003-q1-wph12-02-oct-2021-edexcel-int-as-and-a-level-.png)

Which electrical component is represented by this graph?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The gradient of this graph represent resistance
- Resistance increases with current and therefore with temperature

  - This is the behaviour of a filament lamp

- Make sure to check the axes - this is a *V-I* graph, **not** an *I-V* graph

  - This shape would be a thermistor if the axes were **swapped**
- A diode only conducts in one direction and an Ohmic conductor shows direct proportionality between *V* and *I*, so these two option could be eliminated

parts.problemMd:
The unit of electric potential can be written as $\text{J C}^{-1}$.

Which of the following is the equivalent expression in SI base units?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Start by writing the energy unit, the joule, in SI base units using $E=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

$1 \text{J} = 1 \text{kg m}^{2} \text{s}^{-2}$

- Write the coulomb in SI base units using $Q = I t$

$1 \text{C} = 1 \text{A s}$

- Divide to find the base units of the volt

$1 \text{V} = \frac{\text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2}}{\text{A s}} = \text{kg m}^{2} \text{s}^{-3} \text{A}^{-1}$

**A** is incorrect because these are the base units of the joule only — the denominator $\text{C}^{-1}$ has not been converted.

**B** is incorrect because the coulomb has been replaced by the ampere alone; the factor of $\text{s}$ in $1 \text{C} = 1 \text{A s}$ has been missed.

**D** is incorrect because these are the base units of newton per coulomb (electric field strength), not joule per coulomb — the metre has not been squared.

parts.problemMd:
The graph shows how the potential difference $V$ varies with the current $I$ for a circuit component.

![Graph of potential difference V against current I showing a curve passing through the origin, very flat at low I, then curving steeply upwards as I increases.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/2-waves-and-electricity/current-potential-difference-resistance-and-power/assets/001-graph-of-potential-difference-v-against-current-.png)

Which of the following could be the circuit component?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The gradient of a $V$–$I$ graph at any point is equal to resistance

$R = \frac{V}{I}$

- The curve becomes steeper as $I$ increases, so the resistance increases with current
- As current rises, the filament heats up and the increased lattice vibrations raise the metal's resistance

  - This is characteristic of a filament lamp

**A** is incorrect because an ohmic resistor (at constant temperature) obeys Ohm's law — $V$ is directly proportional to $I$ and the graph would be a straight line through the origin, not a curve.

**C** is incorrect because the resistance of a thermistor (NTC) *decreases* as temperature (and current) increases, so the $V$–$I$ curve would become less steep at higher currents — concave down, not concave up.

**D** is incorrect because a forward-biased diode conducts negligible current until $V$ reaches the threshold (~0.7 V), then $I$ rises sharply for very small further increases in $V$ — on a $V$–$I$ plot the curve is approximately flat above the threshold, not a steeply rising curve through the origin.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For $V$–$I$ graphs, the gradient at any point is the resistance ($R = V / I$). A curve that gets steeper means resistance is increasing — typical of a filament lamp warming up. A curve that gets shallower means resistance is decreasing — typical of an NTC thermistor. Always check the axis order: $I$–$V$ graphs (with $I$ on the vertical axis) and $V$–$I$ graphs (with $V$ on the vertical axis) flip the curvature for the same component.

parts.problemMd:
The unit of resistance is the ohm.

Which of the following is equivalent to the ohm?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- Resistance is calculated using Ohm's law: $R=\frac{V}{I}$

  - 1 volt is equal to 1 joule per coulomb
  - 1 amp is equal to 1 coulomb per second

$\left[\Omega\right] = \frac{V}{A} = \frac{J C^{- 1}}{C s^{- 1}} = J C^{- 2} s$

parts.problemMd: Which of the following derived units can be expressed in SI base units as kg m<sup>2</sup> s<sup>–3</sup> ?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- $P=\frac{E}{t}$ and $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ and $v=\frac{s}{t}$
- Therefore $P = \frac{m v ^{2} }{2 t} = \frac{m ( \frac{s}{t} ) ^{2} }{2 t}$
- The units for this are $[ W ] = [ \frac{k g ( m \frac{ ^{2} }{s} ^{2} ) }{s} ] = [ k g m ^{2} s^{ - } 3 ]$

**A** is incorrect as the base units of the coulomb are As

**B** is incorrect as the base units of the joule are kg m<sup>2 </sup>s<sup>−2</sup>

**C** is incorrect as the base units of the volt are kg m<sup>2 </sup>s<sup>−3</sup> A<sup>−1</sup>

- This could also be done using other expressions, for example $W=Fd$ and $F=ma$

parts.problemMd:
The graph shows how current *I* varies with potential difference *V* for an electrical component.

![q8-wph12-02-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-physics-19/2-waves-and-electricity/current-potential-difference-resistance-and-power/assets/002-q8-wph12-02-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy.png)

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- When potential difference across a diode is in the direction of its forward bias (the right side of the graph), the current should increase sharply with potential difference, as diodes have a low resistance in this direction
- When the direction of potential difference is reversed and is across a diode in reverse bias (the left side of the graph), no current should pass through the diode
- Therefore, the *I-V *graph shown is for a diode
- This is answer **A**

- You will be expected to recognise *I-V* graphs for ohmic and non-ohmic conductors
- The *I-V* graph for a diode has a distinctive shape which you need to be able to recognise and explain

parts.problemMd:
A light dependent resistor (LDR) and a fixed resistor are connected in a circuit, as shown.

The intensity of the light incident on the LDR is increased.

Which of the following does **not** take place as the light intensity is increased?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- As light intensity increases, the current in the circuit increases because the resistance of the LDR decreases

  - This eliminates answer options **A** and **D**
- The potential difference across the fixed resistor will increase as the p.d. across the LDR decreases

  - This eliminates answer option** B**
- Therefore, the total power dissipated in the circuit will not decrease

  - This is because *P = IV* so for the whole circuit, *P = Iε*
  - The current increases, while the emf remains the same, so the power dissipated in the circuit will increase
- Option **C** is the only answer that does not take place

- Examiners reported that many students failed to recognise the word **not** in this question

  - Make sure you read the questions carefully, and underline key words to avoid this type of confusion
  - Is it a good idea to read the question, ask yourself what answer it is looking for, and then read the question again to confirm
